title: Sara won a prized place to study medicine in Glasgow. Why is the Home Office blocking her?
text:
For the last decade, Sara (not her real name), 25, has dreamed of becoming a doctor. She secured a highly sought after place to study medicine at Kabul University in February 2021, but in a matter of months the Taliban returned to power and imposed a ban on women studying for degrees. Sara had been searching for other options. Then the University of Glasgow offered her a lifeline.
Her visa application was made just days before the Home Office introduced a visa brake in March 2026 for students from Afghanistan, Sudan, Myanmar and Cameroon. Her teachers consider her to be an exceptionally able and dedicated student, she had secured funding and the university was waiting to welcome her on to a gateway course at its school of medicine, dentistry and nursing – a route to a full degree course to become a doctor. So why have the UK’s home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, and her officials gone to such extraordinary lengths to bar her?
Sara says her life has been “challenge after challenge”. She survived a suicide bomb attack on her school, swerved her father’s attempts to force her into early marriage, as well as the omnipresent Taliban who patrol Kabul’s streets. Then she made a nail-biting escape from her country and avoided capture by police in Pakistan who were searching for her. But it is the UK’s Home Office, which champions women’s rights, that has inflicted the deadliest blow.
Sara grew up in a poor household in Kabul in the period before the Taliban regained power. Against the wishes of her violent father, who wanted to see her follow the traditional path of teenage marriage and a life of enforced domesticity in service to a husband, she fought to continue her education, encouraged to aim high by inspirational female teachers at her single-sex school.
“The community I come from is a particularly traditional one,” she says. “Even among my relatives I couldn’t find any girl who has been educated. While boys were free, my mum, who has always supported me, was told by relatives that rather than pursuing an education I needed to go somewhere where I could be taught to cook. After a relative’s daughter got married I was told I was next in line.”
But at school, she saw that life could be different. “I was about seven years old when one of my teachers first encouraged us girls,” she says. “Later, my physics teacher was also very supportive. She said that we would face challenges but should never give up in pursuing our dreams.”
Sara says that she is still in contact with some of the girls she was at school with, who were similarly inspired by their female teachers. Some of them are now flying high in other countries, having been granted full university scholarships.
But there were others whose ambitions were thwarted. “I can still see the face of one 15-year-old girl who was like a supportive older sister to me at school. She wanted to continue her education but she was full of tears when she came to school one day and told us her family was forcing her to leave school and get married.”
When Sara was 15, a much-loved uncle died after his heart disease was misdiagnosed. At that moment, she vowed to become a doctor. “My uncle was such a kind soul. He always supported me when my father was being harsh. ‘It’s OK. Whatever your father is doing, I’m with you,’ he used to say to me.”
Sara always put everything into her studies at school, getting marks close to 100% in her tests and exams. Along with her love of science, she speaks multiple languages. She is Hazara and along with Hazaragi speaks Dari, Pashto, Urdu, English, as well as some Spanish and Arabic.
Somehow, despite her father’s disapproval, she continued her studies and attended an educational centre to prepare for Afghanistan’s university entrance exam, the Kankor, so she could secure a place at Kabul University to begin her medical studies. In October 2020, it was targeted by a Taliban suicide bomb attack. She was feeling unwell that day so did not go to school. Many of her friends were killed.
Against the odds, in February 2021, she passed her exam, secured her place at the Kabul University’s medical school, and was overjoyed – until she and other women at the university had their right to study brutally terminated when the Taliban came to power in August 2021.
Devastated, but undeterred from pursuing her dream, she began volunteering at medical clinics in Kabul, taken there and back by clinical staff who supported her, ducking down and hiding in the car when they approached Taliban checkpoints. When Taliban members came to the clinic for treatment, she was bundled into the staff room to hide until they had left. She continued her medical studies at home, begging friends who were studying to send her PDFs of medical textbooks because she couldn’t afford to buy them. She devoured the medical bible Gray’s Anatomy.
Despite the Taliban obstacle, she was determined to keep studying any way she could. “I was at the clinic one day in 2023. I wasn’t allowed to perform medical procedures on patients but wanted to learn as much as I could. I asked a friend to teach me how to do sutures and then practised the technique on a banana. The head surgeon came in and asked what we were doing, saw how enthusiastic I was and allowed me to observe an operation.”
By 2024, life at home with her father was becoming increasingly violent and dangerous and the pressure on Sara to marry was increasing. “The situation was deteriorating so much that we had to find a way to get out,” she says.
Sara hoped she could pursue her medical studies in Pakistan, so before she left Afghanistan she went to the medical school in Kabul to try to get her course records to prove that she had started a medical degree. “Taliban guards wouldn’t let me through the front gate and were very abusive to me so I couldn’t get them,” she says.
Sara was later able to get a reference from one of her lecturers at the university which described her as a “highly dedicated and capable student.”
“She demonstrated strong academic performance, critical thinking and a deep passion for medicine. She is a resilient, compassionate and motivated individual,” the lecturer said.
Sara, her mother, her siblings and other relatives had to leave Afghanistan in a hurry when things reached crisis point with her father. “I could only pack a few clothes,” she says. “But I took my white medical coat with me, hoping that even if I was unable to continue my medical studies in Afghanistan, I would be able to qualify to be a doctor somewhere else.”
The family managed to get together the money to escape to Pakistan by plane. Their cover story was that Sara’s mother needed urgent medical treatment. Their male escort was Sara’s brother-in-law. At Kabul Airport, they were stopped by the Taliban and taken into a room for questioning.
“We arrived at the airport at 12.30pm for a 2pm flight. We were questioned in that room until 1.50pm. My hands were shaking so much. I didn’t think they would let us go. They wanted to know why my father was not accompanying us to Pakistan. When they finally released us at 1.50pm, we all had to run to make it on to the plane before it took off. When we sat on the plane my mum said to us; ‘Our life is full of challenges. If we overcome one, another one comes.’”
Life in Pakistan was not much better. The family overstayed their visa because they had nowhere else to run to and Sara was unable to continue her medical studies. “Sometimes the police came to look for us at the place where we were staying. I hid in the kitchen cupboard when they knocked on our door so they wouldn’t find me,” she says.
A London-based English teacher, Jane Conway, became another lifeline. She taught English to refugee students and became involved in a group called Save Afghan Women. After the Taliban regained power, Conway helped with online English classes for women no longer able to physically study in Afghanistan, and got to know Sara and other members of her family who she supported as they continued their higher education.
It was Conway who found that the University of Glasgow had a gateway course for female students from Afghanistan who wanted to pursue a degree in medicine, and helped her apply. “It was teacher Jane who found this option for me,” says Sara.
She applied for the scheme and was accepted after finding, with Conway’s help, sources of funding to support her with bursaries to cover fees and living expenses. Hope was restored. All she needed now was for the Home Office to grant her a visa to take up the course in Glasgow. She thought that after everything she had been through this would be the easy bit. But three rejections citing contradictory reasons followed.
She was told in one rejection that the Home Office was satisfied she had appropriate funds in place to support her study in the UK although they deemed her not to be a genuine student. She cried and cried at that accusation, after all the years of doing everything possible to pursue her medical studies. “I would like to ask the home secretary what is her definition of a ‘genuine student?’ I wish I had the opportunity to visit her in person and ask her this question face to face, eye to eye.”
Then, in another refusal, they said she didn’t have suitable funds in place, but accepted she was a genuine student.
Sara underwent a phone interview with a Home Office official. “The interview was very tough. It lasted about an hour and a half and the man asked me lots of questions about my mother, my father, my background. After the interview he told me to keep checking my email and I was hopeful I was going to be granted a visa.”
But once again her hopes were dashed. She is now pursuing a degree in accounting and finance in another country, undisclosed for safety reasons, because it is more affordable than a medical course. “I don’t have any other option,” she says.
In London, Conway despairs about the inconsistent decision making by the Home Office. “Sara is a good and wonderful person who wants to do good in the world,” she says. “It would seem that the Home Office is so obsessive in its target seeking that it has become blinded to exceptional cases like Sara’s, denying the UK of the benefits that such motivated and talented people could bring.
“In spite of all the obstacles Sara encountered pursuing her dream to become a doctor, she never gave up. Then, when that wonderful new door of opportunity was opened up to her by the University of Glasgow, instead of walking through it with hope and excitement, it is our British Home Office that unequivocally slams the door shut in her path. I feel a deep shame that the government is cutting off a life-changing opportunity for a truly exceptional person, who has already been persecuted in her own country simply for being a woman.”
On 28 September, Mahmood delighted the audience at the Labour party conference by announcing she was reactivating a refugee resettlement route, albeit a small one, highlighting Afghan women and girls as one of the groups who would benefit. It later emerged that there will be significant restrictions to the scheme for some eligible nationalities (it is only open to Palestinian refugees who have already escaped Gaza and are registered as refugees with the UN, for instance), while the much larger refugee family reunion scheme remains suspended after more than a year.
Sara refuses to give up on her dream of qualifying to become a doctor. She tries to keep up with the latest scientific developments in medicine.
“In Afghanistan, so many people don’t have arms or legs because of all the fighting,” she says. “If I can qualify as a doctor I would like to help people in my country. My ambition is to become a cardiac surgeon because as far as I know there are no female cardiac surgeons in Afghanistan and I would like to be the first.” If she achieves this, she says, “my goal is to use my experiences to inspire other Afghan girls to pursue education and overcome the obstacles in their lives”.
If she can’t ever return to her country, she wants to work with Doctors Without Borders. “They work with people in difficult-to-reach places. I believe that people in those places deserve to have a good doctor to treat them. From my perspective, doctors are superheroes. They are the best for people. Whatever happens, I will always keep my white coat with me. It is the history of my struggle.”
